queue.title: Capital Trusts Evidence, Not Promises
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Reputation is created when a number can be linked to a document, a method, and an accountable person. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Reputation is created when a number can be linked to a document, a method, and an accountable person.

A story can be sold temporarily on the market, but inconsistency can't be financed long-term.

An investor who decides based on promises of future growth, without a documented trail of past decisions and their outcomes, takes on a risk that could have been reduced by a simple request for that history — a request that itself filters serious partners from those with nothing to show.

An organisation seeking serious capital must therefore build a verifiable track record in advance: audited statements, consistent methodology, publicly accessible registers — not as formality, but as the basic precondition for trust that cannot be bought with a promise.

Every important number must have a source, a definition, and a limitation. When they're missing, the investor prices in additional risk.

Transparency isn't weakness. It's the operational advantage of an organisation that knows what it's doing and can prove it.

An organisation seeking serious capital must build a verifiable track record in advance — audited statements, consistent methodology, publicly accessible registers — not as formality, but as the basic precondition for trust that cannot be purchased with a promise.

Building this track record cannot be done retroactively once capital is being sought — it has to be built during the years when no one is asking for it, through consistent reporting practices maintained regardless of whether the organisation currently needs external validation. Organisations that only begin taking disclosure seriously once they need investors are, by definition, too late to have the track record that serious investors are actually looking for.

queue.title: Money Is Information Before It's Capital
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Capital without timely information becomes slow, expensive, and risky. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

In business, money is often viewed only as an amount in an account, a credit line, or investment capacity. That's too narrow. Before it becomes capital, money is information: about liquidity, obligations, risk, timing, and trust.

Management that receives data late is actually managing the past. Even large funds can then be misallocated, blocked, or exposed to unnecessary cost.

Liquidity isn't just a question of how much money exists, but when it's available, under what conditions, and with what level of certainty. That's why a good financial system must link contracts, deadlines, collections, obligations, tax effects, and risk scenarios.

Banks, partners, and investors don't assess only results. They assess data quality, reporting consistency, and management's ability to explain deviations. The more transparent the system, the less room for uncertainty, and uncertainty is always a cost.

Every important financial data point must have a source, a date, an accountable person, and context. Without that, a number isn't management information, it's an assumption.

Capital gives the ability to act. Timely and verifiable information determines whether that ability produces value or risk. That's why information discipline is one of the most important forms of financial discipline.

This framing has practical consequences for how financial data should be handled internally: with the same rigour applied to information security generally, since a financial figure that leaks prematurely or inaccurately can cause damage before a single unit of actual capital has moved.

Before money becomes capital available for investment, it is information about the trust someone else placed in it — forgetting that link makes an organisation prone to spending capital as if it were unconditional.

This framing has practical consequences for how financial data should be handled internally, with the same rigour applied to information security generally, since a figure that leaks prematurely can cause damage before capital has actually moved.

queue.title: Accountability Cannot Be Automated
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Technology can speed up a decision, but accountability must remain tied to a person and institution. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

Technology can speed up a decision, but accountability must remain clearly tied to a person and an institution.

Artificial intelligence, automation, and digital workflow systems can significantly speed up research, data processing, and decision preparation. That's their real value. The problem arises when the tool starts being used as a substitute for accountability.

An algorithm can suggest, compare, and flag. It can't take on legal, financial, or reputational accountability for the final decision. In a serious business system, it must be clear who verified the data, who approved the conclusion, and on what basis the decision was made.

The fastest answer isn't necessarily the best answer. A system that produces a result without a source, context, and the ability to audit it creates a false sense of security. That's why automation must have control points, logged authority, and the ability to roll back to a prior state.

Management's role isn't to manually perform every task, but to set boundaries, rules, and the level of accountability. Technology should improve decision quality, not blur the question of who is accountable for it.

Organisations that understand this won't fear artificial intelligence. They'll use it aggressively for analysis and preparation, but cautiously wherever a decision has legal, financial, or public consequences.

Processes can be automated. Accountability cannot. That distinction determines whether technology becomes an instrument of better governance or a source of new risk.

Automating a workflow can remove repetitive manual steps, but it cannot remove the requirement that someone, specifically named and identifiable, remains responsible for what the workflow produces. Organisations that lose sight of this distinction often end up with systems that are technically well-engineered but organisationally orphaned — no one quite owns the outcome, because everyone assumes the automation itself is somehow accountable. It is not, and treating it as if it were is how avoidable failures go unnoticed until they are large enough to be impossible to ignore.

queue.title: Cybersecurity and Business Continuity
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses cybersecurity and business continuity, key controls, and consequences for recovery readiness.

Securing a business system requires separated access, backups, logs, and a tested recovery plan.

Security is a business function, not just a technical matter. Within the GNK ASG d.o.o. and GNK DINAMO Ltd. system, it must be linked to clear accountability, demonstrable controls, and a documented recovery plan.

Practical implementation includes least-privilege access, multi-factor authentication, separated secrets, change logging, and a tested rollback. Every system must have a process owner, a backup, and a review deadline.

The greatest risk arises when there's a single administrator account, an unverified backup, or a hidden dependency on one individual. Automation and AI can prepare data and alerts, but must not independently make sensitive security decisions.

Resilience isn't proven by a document but by a verified ability to recover. This publication is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

queue.title: Investor Trust Through Transparency
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses investor trust, key transparency practices, and consequences for governance quality.

Investors seek consistent data, explainable decisions, documented risks, and a credible governance structure.

The foundation of this topic is that trust is built through verifiable data. Within the GNK ASG d.o.o. and GNK DINAMO Ltd. business system, this approach must be linked to clear accountability, verifiable data, and documented decisions. Governance quality doesn't depend only on speed, but on the ability to explain, confirm, and later verify every important decision.

Practical implementation begins with a model that includes clear sources, periods, methodology, and risk review. Every element must have a process owner, a data source, an update deadline, and a minimum quality standard.

It's important to distinguish confirmed facts from internal estimates and future projections. Financial, legal, and operational data should carry a date, a source, and context.

Particular attention is needed where results and projections are blended. That risk is reduced by timely reporting, clear authority, and separated approval levels.

Good governance turns a complex topic into a clear operational model. When data is structured, accountability defined, and risks visible, management can act faster without reducing control quality. This publication is part of the GNK ASG Intelligence Desk system and is informational in nature.

queue.title: Cyber Resilience and Continuity
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses cyber resilience and continuity, key controls, and consequences for incident recovery.

Security isn't just preventing an attack. What matters is that an organisation can keep operating, determine what happened, and recover reliably.

A cyber incident can arise from a technical vulnerability, a misconfiguration, a compromised account, or human error. What they share is that consequences grow when there's no prepared response.

Access controls, segmentation, event logging, and backups must be regularly tested. It's not enough for them to exist on paper; they must function in a real incident.

At the moment of an incident, it must be clear who makes technical decisions, who communicates, and who assesses business impact. Unclear authority prolongs downtime.

A continuity plan is only worth as much as it's been tested. Data recovery, backup infrastructure, and contact channels must be available even when the primary system isn't.

For a digital portal, that means separated operational layers, controlled deploys, clear route oversight, verified mail transport, and preserved evidence of changes.

queue.title: Transparent Governance as an Operational Standard
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses transparent governance, key operational practices, and consequences for efficiency and trust.

Trust isn't created by a single statement. It's created when decisions, data, and accountability can be understood and verified.

Transparency is often reduced to publishing annual data. In practice, it's far more important that it's built into everyday work: from receiving a document, through approval, to the final decision and its explanation.

Every important number should have a known origin, a time of creation, and a person or system that confirmed it. Without that, data looks convincing but isn't operationally reliable.

An audit trail isn't an administrative excess. It shows who decided, on what basis, and at what moment. That reduces room for misunderstanding, misinterpretation, and later shifting of blame.

When documents, authority, and statuses are clearly linked, there's less repetition, fewer manual checks, and less downtime. Transparency is therefore not just a reputational value but an efficiency infrastructure.

GNK ASG develops the public and internal layers of its portal precisely on that principle: clear data provenance, separated content categories, and verifiable operational steps.

queue.title: Automation Does Not Remove Accountability
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

A system can execute a rule, but accountability for it still belongs to people and institutions. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A system can execute a rule, send a message, or rank a risk. Accountability for the rule, the data, and the consequences still belongs to people and institutions.

Automation is useful when it removes repetition, speeds up verification, and reduces the chance of accidental error. The problem arises when a technical result starts being presented as a decision with no owner.

Someone must define the system's goal, the permitted data, the boundaries of action, and the correction method. These are governance decisions, not just technical ones.

If a system confirms that an email was sent, the message must actually have been handed to transport. If it was only logged, the user must be given exactly that information.

Every critical process needs the ability to stop, verify, and manually correct. Without that, automation increases speed, but also the consequences of an error.

This principle applies to mail, contact forms, news publishing, and deployment: automation must be verifiable, bounded, and aligned with the actual state.

This principle applies equally to mail systems, contact forms, news publishing, and deployment pipelines: automation must remain verifiable, bounded in scope, and aligned with the actual state of the system it represents.

GNK ASG d.o.o. applies this principle across every automated process it operates, from mail delivery confirmation to news publication governance: each system is designed so that its actual behaviour can be independently verified against what it claims to have done, and a named person remains accountable for reviewing that verification rather than assuming the automation is self-policing.

queue.title: Markets Demand Clear Information
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

The market often punishes ambiguity, delay, and uncredentialed data more than bad news itself. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

The market doesn't only punish bad news. It often punishes ambiguity, delay, and data without a credible source even more strongly.

Capital moves toward places where it can assess risk. When information is incomplete or contradictory, an investor can't distinguish a real problem from a communication failure.

Unclear or inconsistent information reaching the market raises suspicion even when the underlying situation is entirely legitimate — investors and partners react to the clarity of communication as much as to its content.

An organisation that presents its figures consistently, with clear sources and no contradictions between different documents, reduces the room for misinterpretation that could otherwise damage its market standing.

Publishing first isn't the same as publishing reliably. Timeliness matters, but data must be verified and clearly labelled as final, provisional, or estimated.

A number without a period, methodology, and comparison basis can be formally correct but practically misleading. That's why market disclosure must explain its source and limitations.

Equal disclosure rules, stable content categories, and the ability to find earlier information reduce the perception of risk.

That's why a public portal must separate news, official releases, analysis, and authored commentary. A reader must immediately know what they're looking at and who is accountable for the content.

Clarity in this sense is not about simplifying complex information until it loses meaning, but about presenting genuinely complex information in a structure that lets a careful reader actually follow the reasoning, rather than requiring them to take the conclusion on faith.

queue.title: Financial Statement Examples: Croatia
queue.content:
Autor: Nermin Sefić

Nermin Sefić analyses Croatian financial statement standards, deadlines, and practical analysis methods for 2026.

Overview of the balance sheet, profit and loss statement, cash flow statement, and notes to financial statements in Croatia — standards, deadlines, and practical analysis for 2026.

Financial statements are a set of structured documents showing a company's financial position and business results at a given date or over a given period. Every company in Croatia that keeps business records is required to prepare them according to prescribed rules, and the main financial statements include the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, the cash flow statement, the statement of changes in equity, and the notes, prepared under HSFI or IFRS standards.

The filing deadline is 30 April of the current year for the previous business year, and statements are submitted through the RGFI service operated by FINA. This isn't just a formal obligation: analysts, banks, investors, and business partners use these documents to assess creditworthiness and make decisions about cooperation or investment.

The Financial Reporting Standards Board develops and adapts the HSFI standards applied in Croatia, while IFRS is issued by the IASB at the international level. Companies such as Podravka d.d. apply IFRS as adopted by the European Union for their unaudited, non-consolidated statements.

Availability of statements through the RGFI service means any interested user can review the publicly disclosed financial data of Croatian companies. This is particularly useful when analysing business partners or researching the market.

The balance sheet is a static statement because it shows the position on one specific day. Assets comprise non-current assets (real estate, equipment, intangible assets) and current assets (inventory, receivables, cash). Liabilities show the sources of financing: equity, long-term and short-term liabilities.

Key rule: assets must always equal liabilities plus equity. If they don't, there's an error somewhere in the bookkeeping.

This statement shows revenues and expenses for a given accounting period and the operating result. Operating revenue includes revenue from the sale of goods or services, while non-operating revenue can include interest, exchange-rate differences, or revenue from asset sales. Expenses are divided into material costs, wages, depreciation, interest, and other operating costs.

Many analysts consider this statement the most honest mirror of a business. A company can report a profit in the profit and loss statement while simultaneously having serious liquidity problems if customers pay late. The cash flow statement is divided into three categories of activity:

In the period 1–12/2025, Podravka d.d. achieved a net cash flow from operating activities of a positive €35.5 million, while net cash flow from investing activities was a negative €287.6 million, mostly due to the acquisition of Fortenova Group's agricultural companies.

This statement tracks all changes in equity throughout the year: profit or loss shown in the profit and loss statement, dividend payments, capital increases, and revaluation reserves. It's useful for understanding how ownership structure changes and how much profit is retained in the company versus paid out to owners.

“All these statements are interconnected and refer to one another. Viewed together, in their mutual interaction, they speak to a company's state of health, and establishing and understanding that state means having the ability to make appropriate and rational business decisions.” (Group of authors, ed. Lajoš, Ž., 2008.)

Professional advice: Correct recording of financial transactions is the foundation of accurate statements. Sales revenue is recorded on account 7000 (sales revenue) and account 1200 (trade receivables), while wage costs are recorded on account 4000 with a credit to account 1000 (bank). A bookkeeping error carries directly through into every statement.

Croatian companies choose their accounting framework based on entity size and type. Micro and small companies apply HSFI, which is adapted to domestic legislation and somewhat simpler than IFRS. Medium and large companies, as well as those whose securities are traded on a regulated market, are required to apply IFRS. Preparing financial statements under IFRS is more demanding because the IASB issues new standards and amendments every year that can significantly affect the complete financial statements.

The Accounting Act classifies businesses as micro, small, medium, or large based on revenue, assets, and employee-count criteria. Micro entities have the smallest scope of mandatory statements, while large companies must also attach an audit report. Medium-sized companies fall in between: they apply HSFI but have broader disclosure obligations than micro entities.

Since 1 January 2023, the official currency in the Republic of Croatia has been the euro, meaning all financial statements are expressed in euros. The fixed conversion rate was 7.53450 kuna per euro. Older sample notes available online are expressed in kuna and serve only as illustrative material. Currency alignment of statements following Croatia's eurozone entry significantly affects the presentation of financial data and its international comparability.

Professional advice: There's no universal financial statement template that fits every company. Management is ultimately responsible for the truthfulness of the presentation, and experts advise a substantive review of the balance sheet rather than simply relying on ready-made templates. Adapting statements to a company's specific transactions and activity isn't optional, it's an obligation.

Auditors in Croatia most often find the following shortcomings when statements are prepared:

Financial statement analysis isn't just an accounting routine. It's a tool managers, investors, and analysts use to assess a company's financial health, identify risks, and make strategic decisions. The three key analysis methods are horizontal analysis, vertical analysis, and financial ratio analysis.

Horizontal analysis compares the same line items across two or more accounting periods. If sales revenue grows year over year, that can indicate a successful sales strategy. If expenses grow faster than revenue, that's a warning sign, regardless of whether the company still reports a profit.

Example: a company achieved revenue of €400,000 in 2023 and €480,000 in 2024. That's growth of 20%. At the same time, personnel costs rose from €100,000 to €140,000, growth of 40%. That mismatch requires an explanation.

Vertical analysis shows each line item as a percentage of the total. In the profit and loss statement, every expense item is expressed as a share of total revenue, which allows comparison between companies of different sizes or across different years without the influence of absolute amounts.

Financial ratios measure key aspects of a business and are divided into four groups:

Professional analysts use vertical and horizontal analysis to detect abnormalities in time, such as unusual inventory growth or a sudden drop in liquidity, enabling a timely response.

The assumption that the profit and loss statement is the most important statement is a common mistake. That kind of thinking results in insufficient attention to capital structure and cash flow, which can lead to serious gaps in assessing the real financial position. A company can report solid profit while simultaneously having a shortage of net working capital causing illiquidity. Understanding the connection between the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, and the cash flow statement allows for more precise interpretation of results.

For companies with subsidiaries, reviewing consolidated statements is essential for a complete picture. Non-consolidated statements often hide real financial risks that exist at the group level.

Professional advice: Use the results of financial statement analysis for strategic business decisions, not just as accounting reporting. If the analysis shows that storage costs make up a significant share of total expenses, that's a concrete point for reviewing logistics, not just a note in the annual report.

Notes are a mandatory and equal part of the financial statements, not an appendix written at the end. They provide context that the numbers alone can't give: asset valuation methods, going-concern plans, credit-line terms, and everything else needed to understand what stands behind individual line items.

The financial statements of XYZ d.o.o. for a given year are included in the consolidated financial statements prepared by the parent company, which are publicly available through FINA's RGFI service. Such a note immediately tells an analyst that, for the complete picture, they must look at the consolidated data, not just the non-consolidated statements of that one company.

The transition to the euro in 2023 required a specific note on the applied fixed conversion rate of 7.53450 kuna per euro, as well as on how comparative data for the previous year was restated. Companies that omitted this had problems during audits.

Professional advice: The notes are the first document an experienced analyst or auditor reads, not the last. Investors and banks use them to assess creditworthiness, and inadequate notes immediately signal that management doesn't fully understand what it's disclosing. Give them the same attention as the statement tables themselves.

Banks and investors use the notes to verify information not visible from the tables alone. The real-estate valuation method can drastically affect the value of assets, and without the note an analyst doesn't know whether assets are stated at historical cost or a revalued amount. The same applies to inventory: the FIFO method and the average-cost method produce different results when prices change, which directly affects reported profit.

Gnk-asg is a corporate portal that integrates the presentation of financial statements, technology solutions, and market information within the international sports and technology group GNK DINAMO Ltd. The portal publishes detailed financial indicators for the 2025 business year, including revenue of €504 million, along with analyses of capital and liabilities, illustrating how transparent financial reporting works in practice for business partners and investors.

Visit the Gnk-asg portal for insight into corporate financial data and examples of how financial reporting is applied in the real business environment of the sports and technology industry.

Financial statements in Croatia must be prepared under HSFI or IFRS standards, filed by 30 April through FINA's RGFI service, and analysing all five statements together is the only reliable way to assess a company's financial health.
